chapters.title: Chapter 1. The Story of the Door
chapters.text:
Mr Utterson was a lawyer in London. He was a serious man who rarely smiled and never talked much. But his friends liked him, because he was kind and never judged other people too quickly. “I let my brother go to the devil in his own way,” he often said.

Every Sunday Mr Utterson went for a long walk with his cousin, Mr Richard Enfield. They did not seem to have much in common, and they often walked for an hour without saying a word. However, both men looked forward to these walks all week.

One Sunday they walked down a busy little street in a pleasant part of the city. On one side of the street there was an old building with no windows, only a dark door with no bell or knocker. The door looked dirty and neglected.

Enfield pointed at it with his stick. “Have you ever noticed that door?” he asked. “It is connected in my mind with a very strange story.”

“Really?” said Utterson. “What story?”

“I was coming home at about three o’clock one winter morning,” Enfield began. “The streets were completely empty. Suddenly I saw two people. One was a small man who was walking fast. The other was a girl of eight or ten who was running along a side street. They ran into each other at the corner. And then something horrible happened. The man calmly walked over the child’s body and left her screaming on the ground.

“I ran after him and brought him back. A crowd had already gathered around the girl. Everyone hated the man at first sight, even the doctor. I have never seen such anger in people’s faces. We told him that we would destroy his name all over London unless he paid the family a hundred pounds.

“He agreed, and where do you think he took us? To that door. He went in with a key and came back with ten pounds in gold and a cheque for the rest. The cheque was signed by a very well-known and respected man. I was sure it was false, but the next morning the bank paid it.”

“What was the man’s name?” asked Utterson.

“Hyde. Edward Hyde.”

“And what does he look like?”

“That is hard to say,” answered Enfield. “There is something wrong with his appearance, something unpleasant, but I cannot say exactly what. I have never seen a man I disliked so much.”

Utterson was silent for a while. He already knew the name on the cheque. And he knew the name Hyde too, because he had read it in a document in his own office.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. Searching for Mr Hyde
chapters.text:
That evening Mr Utterson went home, opened his safe and took out a document. It was the will of his old friend and client, Dr Henry Jekyll. The will said that if Dr Jekyll died or disappeared for more than three months, all his money and property would go to “his friend and benefactor Edward Hyde”.

Utterson had always disliked this will. Before, he had worried because he knew nothing about Mr Hyde. Now he worried because he knew too much.

“I thought it was madness,” he said to himself, “but now I begin to fear it is disgrace.”

He went to see Dr Lanyon, a doctor who had been friends with both him and Jekyll for many years. But Lanyon had never heard of Hyde. He said that he and Jekyll had not been close for ten years. “Jekyll has become too strange for me,” he said. “He has been doing unscientific experiments.”

That night Utterson could not sleep. He kept imagining the small man walking over the child. From then on, he began to watch the door in the little street. He went there in the morning before work, at lunchtime and late at night.

“If he is Mr Hyde,” he thought, “I shall be Mr Seek.”

At last, on a cold, dry night, he heard light footsteps. A small man, plainly dressed, walked straight to the door and took out a key. Utterson stepped forward and touched his shoulder.

“Mr Hyde, I think?”

Hyde stepped back with a hissing sound, but he answered calmly. “That is my name. What do you want?”

“I am an old friend of Dr Jekyll’s. May I see your face?”

After a moment Hyde turned towards him. Utterson looked at him carefully. There was no single thing wrong with his face, yet Utterson felt disgust and fear.

“How do you know me?” Hyde asked.

“We have common friends. Dr Jekyll, for example.”

“He never told you about me!” cried Hyde angrily. “You have lied.” Then, with a wild laugh, he unlocked the door and disappeared into the house.

The building was actually the back of Dr Jekyll’s house, where his old laboratory stood. Utterson walked round to the front door and asked Poole, Jekyll’s butler, about Mr Hyde. Poole said that Hyde had a key and that the servants had orders to obey him.

Utterson walked home with a heavy heart. “Poor Harry Jekyll,” he thought. “He is in deep trouble. This Hyde must know some secret from his past. If he learns about the will, he may even want to kill Jekyll to get the money sooner.”

chapters.title: Chapter 3. The Carew Murder
chapters.text:
Two weeks later Dr Jekyll gave a dinner for some old friends, and Utterson stayed behind after the others had gone. He decided to speak openly.

“I have been wanting to talk to you about your will,” he said. “I have learned something about young Hyde.”

Jekyll’s handsome face went pale. “I do not want to hear any more,” he said. “You do not understand my position. It is a very strange one. But I can tell you this: the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr Hyde. I promise you that. Please, just help him if I am gone.”

Utterson unwillingly agreed.

Nearly a year later, in October, London was shocked by a terrible crime. Late one night a maid was looking out of her window at the moonlit street. She saw an old gentleman with white hair speaking politely to a small man. She recognised the small man. It was Mr Hyde, who had once visited her master. Suddenly Hyde began to shout, and then he hit the old man with his heavy stick again and again, like a madman. The old man fell and died in the street. When the maid woke up from her faint, Hyde had gone.

The dead man was Sir Danvers Carew, a well-known member of Parliament. In his pocket there was a letter addressed to Mr Utterson. That was why the police came to the lawyer early the next morning.

Utterson looked at the broken stick and recognised it at once. He had given it to Henry Jekyll as a present many years ago. He took the police officer, Inspector Newcomen, to Hyde’s rooms in Soho.  Everything had been thrown about, as if someone had left in a hurry. The police found the other half of the stick behind the door, and some burnt papers in the fireplace. But Hyde had disappeared completely.

That afternoon Utterson visited Jekyll. He found the doctor in his laboratory, sitting by the fire. He looked very ill.

“Have you heard the news?” Utterson asked. “You have not been mad enough to hide this man, have you?”

“Utterson, I swear to God I will never see him again,” cried Jekyll. “I have finished with him. He is safe, and he will never be heard of again.”

He showed Utterson a letter signed by Hyde. It said that Hyde had a safe way to escape. Later, Utterson’s clerk, Mr Guest, who was an expert on handwriting, compared this letter with a note from Jekyll. The two were almost the same, only sloping in different directions.

“Henry Jekyll forged a letter for a murderer!” thought Utterson, and his blood ran cold.

chapters.title: Chapter 4. The Death of Dr Lanyon
chapters.text:
Time passed, and there was no news of Mr Hyde. The police had offered a large reward, but he seemed to have disappeared from the face of the earth. People learned many terrible things about his past, but nobody knew where he was.

With Hyde gone, Dr Jekyll became a new man. He came out of his lonely life and visited his friends again. He gave dinners and did a lot of good work for the poor. For more than two months he was at peace.

On the eighth of January Utterson had dinner at Jekyll’s house with a small group of friends, and Lanyon was there too. Jekyll looked from one to the other, just like in the old days when the three of them were inseparable. But on the twelfth, and again on the fourteenth, the door was closed to Utterson. “The doctor is not seeing anyone,” said Poole.

Worried, Utterson went to see Lanyon. He was shocked by his friend’s appearance. In a few days Lanyon had changed from a healthy man into a dying one. He had grown thin and old, and there was deep fear in his eyes.

“I have had a shock,” Lanyon said, “and I shall never recover. It is only a question of weeks.”

“Jekyll is ill too,” said Utterson. “Have you seen him?”

Lanyon’s face changed. “I do not want to see or hear of Dr Jekyll again,” he said in a trembling voice. “I regard that person as dead.”

Three weeks later Dr Lanyon died. After the funeral, Utterson locked himself in his office and opened an envelope that Lanyon had left for him. Inside there was another envelope with the words: “Not to be opened till the death or disappearance of Dr Henry Jekyll.”

“Disappearance” again, just like in the will. Utterson wanted very much to open it, but he was a man of honour. He put the envelope back in his safe.

He tried to visit Jekyll several times, but Poole always sent him away. “The doctor stays in his laboratory all the time,” Poole said. “He sometimes even sleeps there.”

One Sunday Utterson and Enfield were walking past the little door again. They looked up at the laboratory window and saw Jekyll sitting there like a sad prisoner. They began to talk to him kindly and invited him to come for a walk. He smiled and started to answer, but suddenly the smile disappeared. An expression of such terror came over his face that the blood froze in their veins. The window was closed immediately.

The two men walked away in silence. “God forgive us,” said Utterson at last.

chapters.title: Chapter 5. The Last Night
chapters.text:
One evening in March, as Mr Utterson was sitting by the fire after dinner, Poole came to see him.

“Mr Utterson, something is wrong,” he said. “I think there has been foul play. Please come with me.”

When they arrived at Jekyll’s house, they found all the servants standing together in the hall. Poole led Utterson through the garden to the laboratory.

“Sir, Mr Utterson is here to see you,” he called.

A voice answered from inside. “Tell him I cannot see anyone.”

Poole took Utterson back to the kitchen. “Sir,” he said, “was that my master’s voice?”

“It seemed very changed,” answered the lawyer.

“I have worked in this house for twenty years. That was not his voice. My master was killed eight days ago, when we heard him cry out. And who is in there instead of him, and why he stays there, is a question for heaven!”

For a whole week, Poole explained, the person in the room had been sending out notes, asking for a certain chemical. The servants went to every chemist in London, but each time the note came back. “This powder is not pure,” it said. “Find me more of the old kind.”

“And one day,” said Poole, “I saw him in the laboratory, looking for something among the boxes. He cried out like a rat and ran back into the room. Sir, he was small, and he wore a mask on his face. If that was my master, I will eat my hat. I believe it was Mr Hyde.”

Utterson decided that they had to break down the door. They took an axe and went to the laboratory. They could hear footsteps inside, going up and down, up and down, all the time.

“Jekyll,” cried Utterson, “I demand to see you!”

“Utterson,” said the voice, “for God’s sake, have mercy!”

“That is not Jekyll’s voice. It is Hyde’s! Down with the door, Poole!”

Poole swung the axe. The door shook, and a scream of pure animal terror came from the room. At the fifth blow the door fell in. And on the floor lay the body of a man, still moving a little. It was Edward Hyde, dressed in clothes much too big for him. He had taken poison and was dead.

They searched every corner of the building, but they found no trace of Henry Jekyll, alive or dead. On the desk there was a large envelope addressed to Utterson. Inside were a new will, which now left everything to Utterson himself, and a short note from Jekyll. It asked him to read Lanyon’s letter first, and then Jekyll’s own confession.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. Dr Lanyon’s Letter
chapters.text:
Utterson went home and, with shaking hands, opened Lanyon’s letter. This is what he read.

“On the ninth of January I received a letter from my old friend Henry Jekyll. He asked me to go to his laboratory, take a certain drawer from his cabinet and bring it to my house. At midnight, he wrote, a man would come in his name, and I had to give him the drawer. My life, my honour and my reason depend on you, he wrote.

“I thought he was mad, but I did what he asked. The drawer contained some white salt, a small bottle of red liquid and a notebook. The notebook was a list of dates over many years, with short notes like ‘double’ and, once, ‘total failure!!!’

“At midnight a small man came to my door. His clothes were far too large for him, and I felt a strange disgust when I looked at him. He was terribly excited.

“‘Have you got it?’ he cried. When he saw the drawer, he gave a sob of relief. He asked for a glass, and he mixed the salt with the red liquid. It changed colour from red to purple and then to green.

“Then he looked at me. ‘Now,’ he said, ‘will you let me take this glass and leave your house without asking any questions? Or has your curiosity become too strong? Think before you answer. If you choose to stay, a new world of knowledge and power will open before your eyes.’

“‘I have gone too far to stop now,’ I said. ‘I want to see the end.’

“‘Very well, Lanyon. Remember your promise to keep this secret. You have always laughed at my science. Now look!’

“He put the glass to his lips and drank it all at once. He cried out and held on to the table. His eyes stared. His face seemed to melt and change. His body grew bigger. The next moment I jumped back against the wall, with my arm raised to protect me.

“‘O God!’ I screamed, again and again. There in front of me, pale and shaking, like a man returning from death, stood Henry Jekyll!

“What he told me in the next hour, I cannot write down. I saw what I saw, I heard what I heard, and my soul is sick with it. My life has been shaken to its roots. I cannot sleep, and I feel that I shall die soon. I will say only one thing, Utterson. The creature who came to my house that night was, by Jekyll’s own confession, the man known as Hyde, the murderer of Carew.

“Hastie Lanyon”

chapters.title: Chapter 7. Henry Jekyll’s Statement
chapters.text:
Last, Utterson opened Jekyll’s own confession.

“I was born rich and healthy, and I wanted the respect of good people. But I also had a strong love of pleasure, and I hid it carefully. So from a young age I lived a double life. Slowly I understood a great truth: man is not truly one, but truly two. There is good and evil in every one of us, and they are always at war.

“I began to dream of separating them. What if the evil side could live in one body and the good side in another? Then each could go its own way, free of the other.

“After long experiments I made a drug. I knew it was dangerous, but late one night I mixed it and drank it. I felt terrible pain, then something new and sweet. I felt younger, lighter and happier, and I knew that I had become wicked, ten times more wicked. When I looked in the mirror, I saw Edward Hyde for the first time. But I did not hate him. He was myself.

“I drank the drug again and became Jekyll once more. Now, as Hyde, I could enjoy my secret pleasures, and then, as Dr Jekyll, wash my hands of them.

“But Hyde grew crueller and stronger. One morning I woke up in my own bed and looked at my hand. It was not my hand. It was small, hairy and dark. I had become Hyde in my sleep, without the drug! From that moment, changing back became harder and harder. Sometimes I needed a double dose.

“I decided to choose Jekyll, and for two months I did not touch the drug. But then I was weak. I drank it again, and Hyde came out roaring. That night he killed Sir Danvers Carew, and he felt only joy. Afterwards I swore never to become Hyde again.

“Then, one fine January day, I was sitting in Regent’s Park when I felt the change come over me without any drug. I was Hyde in the middle of the city, with the police looking for me everywhere. That was why I needed Lanyon’s help.

“Since then Hyde returns whenever I sleep or relax. I have almost no powder left, and the new salt does not work. The first salt was impure, and I cannot get it again.

“This is my last hour as Henry Jekyll. Soon I shall become Hyde forever. Will he die on the scaffold, or will he find the courage to free himself? I do not know, and I do not care. Here I lay down the pen, and bring the life of that unhappy Henry Jekyll to an end.”
